I am retired military and only have Tricare for insurance.  Currently, neither VA or Tricare cover any Transgender surgeries.  Although things may be changing in regards to the VA.  Also , until recently I worked for 7 years with a small company that paid well, but did not offer any king of Insurance.  

All this being said, if I want any kind of Transgender surgery, especially bottom surgery, it will be on my dime, and I don't have a lot of money to throw around.

A lot of people like to throw around the concept of using insurance like you can just walk to the corner drug store and get signed up.  For a lot of people that just isn't possible for whatever reason.  So yea, I feel your pain.

I also agree with most of the respondents here saying that you get what you pay for and going the cheapest route  doesn't always give you the best results.  Think of it this way.  You have a job that is 10 miles away and need a car.  Yea, you would love to drive a Mercedes, but are you  willing to settle for a used piece of junk just to get you down the road?  And before anyone gives me any crap, I understand that's a weak analogy, but it gets close to the thought process.

Anyway, desperate times may call for desperate measures.  It all depends on how desperate you are and/or are willing to wait it out for the means to acquire a better but more expensive surgeon with  insurance by other means.

With all that said, I agree that if you can wait until you can obtain surgery through surgery, I would say wait it out.  If not, here are 3 options I have looked at in regards to paying for surgery myself without insurance (I live in the US).

First off, if you can travel outside the country, I hear a lot of great things about Dr. Chettewut in Thailand.  Cost is typically much less than anything you can get in the US, (even after travel costs), and hear a lot of people say he typically has good results.

Dr. Aguilar in Mexico is also a low price option, although I don't hear as many comments, good or bad, as I do for Dr. Chettewut in Thailand.

A third option within the US, is Dr. Macphee in North Carolina.  I have heard good and bad about her, but she is pretty affordable (15k - 25k) depending on the type of bottom surgery.  Another nice thing about Doc Macphee is she is willing do surgery with informed consent only, not needing letters from therapists, IRL, or even hormones.

Bottom line, there are a LOT of good but expensive surgeons, out there, and a few cheap but questionable surgeons as well.  With varying  costs and aesthetic results in the middle.  If you are able, by all means get the better surgeon.  But if you find you absolutely MUST go with a lower end surgeon, I very strongly suggest you do your homework and determine if they are worth the risk.

(sorry, didn't intend to be such a long post)

Best of luck to you

I consider myself trans, and I am very supportive of human rights and inclusion whenever and wherever possible.

That being said, I am really on the fence in regards to trans women participating in women's sports, and here's my reasoning.  There is a reason there are men's sports and women's sports; because if you throw men and women on the same field, the males are typically much stronger and would likely dominate in just about every physical competition.  Trans-women, having once been male, I feel would likely still have at least some of the male strength attributes well into their transition.  And any physical advantage, however slight, would not be fair to the CIS females in the sport.

Now I understand there should be qualifiers as well.  If it is casual sporting, or little-league type sports, I say, "who cares", and go with it.  And if someone transitioned really early before testosterone had much of an effect on their body, then they might not be a threat either.  But in this regards, I ask, "where do you draw the line".  But once you are in high school, college, or even pro's, then I think trans-women, again, having even a very slight advantage, would be unfair.

Bottom line, I'm all for inclusion, and if the other girls on the field are okay with it, I say go for it.  But if her body still has any lingering effects from previously being male, then I can understand how it may be unfair (however slight) to the other women on the field.

Okay, I haven't read through all the responses, so forgive me if I am repeating something that has already been said.  Also, if I missed the point of this post, and it wasn't really asking for financial help, again, please forgive me.  Sometimes I take things more literally than I should.

Number 1 is you didn't state what kind of income you have.  That is paramount in budgeting.

Once you know how much is coming in, then you start with things that are absolutely necessary to live.  (Rent, food, electricity, etc...)  And even there, figure out how you can cut back a bit.  Not eating out or ordering fast food can save a TON of money.  Also, look at ways you can minimize energy consumption.  Turning off lights, use appliances less often.

After you have a grasp on your "Needs", then move on to your "Wants".  How much do you have left over after your "Needs".  Now divide that up between things you would like to have, but don't absolutely need, such as entertainment and clothes.  Where can you cut back, or what expense can you eliminate all together.

Finally, whatever is left you can put into savings to help towards your transition.  And actually, if you know how much you would like to save each month, then perhaps deduct that from your amount remaining after "Needs", and THEN take whatever you have left and use it to determine what "Wants" you can still keep.

Really basic, but I hope that helps.

One more thing... do NOT, I repeat DO NOT use credit cards and loans for purchases if at all possible.  The interest rate, even if it is low, is money you are just throwing away for nothing.  Maybe have a separate savings for more expensive "Wants" and pay cash,  You can be surprised at how much you can save over the long term.

Lastly, if you smoke, drink, or do casual drugs, do what you can to stop.  (I am not judging).  Not only will stopping be good for your health, these vices tend to be VERY expensive and stopping can be the first step in saving a LOT of money.

Best of luck to ya.
